newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU births hit postwar low, statisticians say.
newsitem.headline: EU births hit postwar low, statisticians say.

text.p: Women in the 15 European Union states had fewer babies last year than in any year since 1945, leaving immigrants to account for most of the bloc's population growth, an EU study released on Monday showed.
With fewer than four million babies born in 1995, the EU's fertility rate hit a postwar low of 1.43 children per woman, the EU statistics office Eurostat said.
That means that if present patterns continue, each woman living in the EU will produce an average of 1.43 children during her lifetime. That compares with an average of 1.5 during the period 1990-94.
"It all relates to modern lifestyles or behaviour," Harri Cruysen, project leader for demographic projections at Eurostat, told Reuters.
He said some southern countries were now following a pattern that was seen earlier in northern countries, with women having fewer babies as they spend more time in school and in jobs.

Italy had the lowest fertility rate in 1995, at 1.17 children per women, followed by Spain with 1.18. That compares with a high of 1.87 in Ireland, where Cruysen said the rate was influenced partly by Catholic teachings.
In explaining the low number of EU births, Cruysen said modern couples are also fussier about selecting partners and are not as quick to jump into marriage as earlier generations.
Housing is also a problem in many EU countries, prompting young people to live longer with their parents, he said.
The EU's population grew in 1995, however, by just over one million persons to 372,662,100, Eurostat said. Net immigration represented 75 percent of the increase, the highest percentage since 1945.

The trend was most marked in Germany and Italy, both of which would have lost population without immigration. Germany's natural population fell by 115,500, while net immigration stood at 421,900 -- by far the highest inflow of people in the EU.
That was partly the result of Germany's policy of allowing free entry for immigrant ethnic Germans from eastern Europe.
The figures also show that French baby girls have the longest life expectancy in the EU -- almost 82 years -- although analysts are not completely sure why.

"That's a very difficult question for everybody," Cruysen said. "It seems that French women take a lot of care of their lives, their bodies, they spend a lot of time with the doctor," he said. French baby boys are not so lucky -- their life expectancy is only 73.8 years.
Baby boys have the best chance for a long life in Sweden, where they can expect to live 76.1 years.
The overall EU life expectancy at birth fell slightly in 1995 to 80.1 years for women and 73.7 for men.
The figures are based on 1995 mortality rates and may have been influenced by an influenza outbreak in some northern countries, along with the unusually hot summer, Cruysen said.
